title: A contact path for a law practice
metaTitle: Law practice contact page that earns a reply
excerpt: A law practice contact page should say what happens next, how fast you reply, and what to have ready. Ten fields lose a client who has a deadline.
alt: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens on a wall, a map of steps in the way a contact page should show what happens after someone writes.
caption: Screens on a wall, connected in order, so the path is visible. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a law firm contact page say up front?
faqs.answer: Say what happens after they write, who reads it, and how fast a person replies on a normal week. Say that the first reply is about fit and conflicts, not legal advice, and that they are not engaged yet. A client with a deadline can plan around a true sentence.

faqs.question: Which fields belong on the first form?
faqs.answer: Ask for the kind of matter, the deadline, a name, a way to reply, and the other party's name if you need it for a conflict check. Let the document follow by email if phone uploads stall. Leave referral sources and long life stories for later.

faqs.question: Why are long intake forms a problem?
faqs.answer: Each extra field is a pause, and people often leave a page within 10 to 20 seconds when the value is unclear. A ten-field form feels like an application for help they have not been offered. Collect the formal facts in the engagement letter, after a human has said the matter fits.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A law practice contact page should tell a client choosing counsel under time pressure what happens after they reach out, how fast a person replies, and what to have ready. The action is to request a consultation. A form with ten fields is a way to lose them before anyone has read a word.

They already decided your matter might fit, or they would not be here. The page has one job left: make the ask small, and make the next hour predictable. Nielsen Norman Group's 2011 research is a fair clock for this moment. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and they read only about a quarter of the text on pages they open. The quarter they read should be the promise of a reply, not your postal address in triplicate.

## What happens after they reach out

Write the sequence in three or four sentences at the top, before the form.

They send the kind of matter, a way to reach them, and the deadline. A person at the firm reads it on business days, or whatever the true window is. You reply with whether you can act, whether there is a conflict you can already see, and how a consultation gets booked. That reply is not legal advice, and it does not mean they have engaged you yet.

Name the role that reads the form if you can. "A solicitor reads new matters" is better than "the team." If a coordinator screens for conflicts and deadlines first, say that, and say they are not giving legal advice. Clients forgive a short path. They do not forgive a void.

Say what you will not do in the first reply. You will not review the whole lease in the confirmation email. You will not tell them to sign or not sign before you have the papers and a proper instruction. That limit is part of being careful, and it belongs where they are about to hit send.

If you have two paths, label them. Ordinary consultations through the form. A staffed phone line for matters that cannot wait until the next business morning, with the hours and what counts as that kind of matter. Mixing them produces panic in a queue and routine work treated like a siren.

## How fast, said in a way you can keep

Publish a speed you have already kept, not a speed that sounds attentive. "We reply the same business day when the note arrives before three, and the next business day otherwise" is a real promise if it is true. "We respond promptly" is a mood. A client with a signing date cannot plan on a mood.

If you are slow during court weeks or holidays, say so on the page when those periods are known, or build the promise around business days so you do not imply a Sunday reply you will not make. Updating the sentence for a two-week closure is better than an auto-reply that contradicts the website.

Do not print "within the hour" because a competitor did. Google's helpful-content guidance weighs trust heavily on topics that affect a person's safety or finances, and a missed promise is a trust failure before the matter starts. Choosing counsel is that kind of topic. A slower true sentence beats a fast false one.

The confirmation screen should repeat the speed. "You will hear from us by the next business day at the email you gave." Include the address they can write to if the form fails. A client who just attached a letter needs to know it landed.

## What to have ready

Tell them what to gather before they type, in a short list beside the form. The list lowers the chance they abandon halfway through to go find a PDF.

For most matters, four things are enough to request time.

- The kind of matter, in a sentence. Shop lease, termination letter, owner dispute.
- The deadline, even if it is only "the other lawyer asked for a reply by Friday."
- A way to reply, email or phone, and the name they want used.
- The other party's name, when you need it to see if you can act at all.

The document itself can be optional on the first send if attaching files on a phone is where people stall. You can ask them to bring the lease to the consultation, or to reply to your email with it. If you do require the file, say the formats you accept and a size that will actually send.

Do not ask how they heard about you, their budget, their date of birth, or a paragraph titled "tell us your story" before you have offered a time. Those questions serve the firm. The client is trying to get a yes or a no on fit. Story belongs in the consultation, where a person can listen.

Conflict questions should be the minimum that lets you refuse early. The other side's name is often that minimum. A full corporate family tree can wait until you know the matter is one you might take.

## The form itself

Keep the fields to the list above. Each field needs a visible label, not a placeholder alone. W3C's WCAG overview describes a standard that applies to forms and to mobile, organized around pages that are perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A label that vanishes when they type fails the first of those, and it fails anyone who gets interrupted and comes back.

Mark what is required, and make the required set small. If the deadline is unknown, let them say unknown. If they have no file yet, let them send the sentence anyway.

Group the fields in the order they think. Matter. Deadline. Name. Email. Other party. A notes box of a few lines, optional. The button says "Request a consultation," the same words as the rest of the site. "Submit" is what a database says.

Show errors next to the field, in text, after they try to send. Do not clear the form. Do not rely on color alone. Let them fix an email typo without starting over.

On a phone, the button sits where the thumb is, large enough to hit, and it stays visible after the keyboard opens. Test that. Many forms hide the button behind the keyboard and the client thinks the page is broken.

After a successful send, do not dump them on a generic thank-you with a newsletter pitch. Repeat the sequence. Offer the email address. Do not start a hard sell for a different service.

## Ten fields is how you lose a deadline

Count the fields on the current page. If there are ten, you are interviewing them for a job they have not been offered.

Typical extras that feel reasonable inside the firm and expensive outside it: title, company number, postal address, preferred office, referral source, marketing consent, a second phone, a dropdown of twenty practice areas that do not match their words, a captcha that fails twice, and a terms PDF that must be opened before the button works.

Each extra field is a chance to go find information they do not have in the hallway. Nielsen's account is that the first seconds are when people decide to stay. A form that looks like an application fails that test even if the headline was clear.

Cut to the consultation request. You can ask the rest once a human is in the thread and the client has a reason to answer. The engagement letter can carry the formal facts. The website does not have to be the engagement letter.

If a regulator or an insurer requires a specific warning near the form, put the warning in readable text near the button, short enough to finish. A wall of disclaimer above the only action teaches them you are more interested in covering the firm than in hearing the deadline.

## The rest of the page, in order

Under or beside the form, in this order:

The sequence and the speed, if they were not above. The list of what to have ready. The address and the hours, for people who will visit. A named person or a role. A link back to the matters you take, so someone who landed here from search can still check fit.

A map is useful when visiting the office is part of the decision. It is not a substitute for the reply promise. Do not let an interactive map push the form below the first screen on a phone. Address in text is more useful than a pin when they are copying it into another app, and it is more reliable for someone who cannot use the map.

The phone number, if you publish one, needs hours and a sentence about what it is for. A number that rings to a voicemail nobody checks is worse than no number. Email should be a real address a person reads, repeated as text so it can be copied when the form fails.

## Before you publish the path

Send the form to yourself from a phone. Confirm the email that arrives contains the matter, the deadline, and a return address. Confirm the sender saw the promise you intended, not a blank page. Reply to that test the way you claim you reply, and see if the speed is true.

Ask a colleague to request a consultation for a pretend shop lease due on Friday. Count their fields and their hesitations. If they stop to ask you what "matter reference" means, the label is wrong. If they apologize for not attaching a file you did not need, the page made them feel unprepared. Change the page.

Then read the site for costume one last time. The contact page is a poor place to rediscover marble and a Latin sign-off. The client is trying to hand you a deadline. Take it plainly.

Once this path is short, the useful edit is often subtraction on the rest of the site. Read [what to leave off the site](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-a-law-practice) before you add a new banner above the form.

When you want help making the path this direct on your own site, look at [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The contact page should be the simplest page you publish.
